questions.stem: A legal-operations director wants a Claude agent that pulls renewal dates, liability caps and termination clauses out of supplier contracts. She asks the team to skip a long discovery phase and "just start building". You have two weeks before the design review and want to finish discovery with real evidence that the approach is feasible. Which approach is MOST effective?

options.text: Run stakeholder workshops to capture every requirement in a full specification, get it signed, and start prototyping only after sign-off.
With contract specialists, label a small set of real contracts including hard cases, agree thresholds, and test a time-boxed prototype on them.
Build the production extraction pipeline straight away, put it in front of the legal team, and treat the first month in production as the feasibility test.
Have Claude generate several hundred synthetic contracts with known answers, so a large test set is ready without waiting for access to real contracts.

questions.explanation: Discovery should end with **evidence**, not only documents. A small labelled set of *real* contracts (with the hard cases the specialists know about), agreed thresholds and a quick prototype run against them show whether the approach can work before design money is spent. The same set then seeds the eval suite for every later phase.

whyWrong.A: A big specification without any test against real documents still leaves feasibility unknown, and it delays the evidence the sponsor actually needs.
whyWrong.C: Using production as the feasibility test exposes users to an unvalidated system and gives no agreed baseline to judge results against.
whyWrong.D: Synthetic contracts miss the messiness of real ones (scans, amendments, odd wording). They can supplement a test set but cannot replace real labelled examples.

questions.mindset: End discovery with a small, real, labelled example set and a measured prototype, not just a requirements document.

questions.stem: In the design phase of an internal policy assistant, two senior engineers have argued for three weeks. One wants to put the whole 150-page policy manual into every prompt. The other wants a retrieval pipeline. Discovery produced a labelled question set and agreed targets for accuracy, latency and cost per question. What should the architect do to settle the decision in the MOST defensible way?

options.text: Choose retrieval now, since it will scale better if the manual grows, and record that rationale in the design document.
Choose the full-manual prompt now because the manual fits in the context window and simpler is usually better; revisit only if users complain.
Ask Claude to compare the two designs in a written analysis and adopt whichever approach its reasoning finds more robust.
Prototype both, run each on the labelled question set against the agreed targets, and record the choice and evidence in an ADR.

questions.explanation: The design phase uses the eval suite from discovery to **choose between options**. Running both candidates on the same labelled set against the agreed targets turns an opinion fight into a measured decision. Writing it up in an architecture decision record (ADR) keeps the evidence for later owners and future revisits.

whyWrong.A: Scaling for a growth that may never happen is a guess. It may add cost and complexity the current requirements don't need.
whyWrong.B: Simplicity is a good default and the manual may well fit, but choosing without measuring against the targets, and revisiting only if users complain, skips the evidence that design is supposed to produce.
whyWrong.C: A model's written opinion is not evidence about this data. The question set already gives a direct, measurable way to compare the designs.

questions.mindset: When options are disputed, let the eval suite decide and document the evidence in an ADR.

questions.stem: Your team is about to transfer ownership of a document-triage agent to the client's operations team. The documentation is delivered and a walkthrough has been held. Before the formal transfer, what is the STRONGEST evidence that the receiving team can actually run the system?

options.text: Working alone, the receiving team runs the eval suite on a proposed change and resolves a simulated incident from the runbook.
Each lead on the receiving team signs a form confirming they have read the architecture document, the runbook and the eval guide.
The build team records a detailed video walkthrough of every component so the receiving team can watch any of them at any time.
The build team stays the main on-call contact for the next quarter while the receiving team watches how incidents are handled.

questions.explanation: A good handoff exit criterion is **demonstrated ability**: the new owners use the eval suite and the runbook on their own. A drill shows gaps in the documents while the build team is still around to fix them.

whyWrong.B: A signed form shows the documents were read, not that the team can use them under pressure.
whyWrong.C: Videos help people learn, but they don't show the team can operate the system. Watching is not the same as doing.
whyWrong.D: Watching for a quarter delays real ownership and still never tests whether the receiving team can act alone.

questions.mindset: Handoff is done when the new owners prove they can run evals and handle an incident themselves.

questions.stem: A consultancy built a client's service with Claude Code. Two things kept the consultants productive: a repeatable release-review workflow they invoked before every release, and a PreToolUse hook that blocked edits to anything under infra/secrets/. Both lived in each consultant's personal ~/.claude/skills folder and ~/.claude/settings.json. After handoff, the client's engineers report that the review workflow does not exist for them and the hook never fires. What is the BEST fix with the fewest moving parts?

options.text: Send each client engineer the consultants' personal skill folder and settings file, and ask them to copy both into their own ~/.claude directory.
Put the workflow steps in a CLAUDE.local.md and the hook in .claude/settings.local.json at the repository root, so they load for anyone working in that checkout.
Move the workflow into a project skill under .claude/skills and the hook into the project's .claude/settings.json, and commit both to the repository.
Write the review steps and the rule 'never edit files under infra/secrets/' into the project CLAUDE.md, which Claude Code loads automatically for every engineer.

questions.explanation: Team knowledge should travel **with the repository**. A project skill (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) is meant to be committed so the whole team gets it, and a committed .claude/settings.json gives everyone who clones the repo the same permissions, hooks and plugins. Both are versioned with the code, so they stay in step as the system changes. Personal files under ~/.claude belong to one person and are not part of a handoff.

whyWrong.A: Copies in each person's home folder are not versioned with the code, drift apart as soon as someone edits theirs, and never reach the next engineer who joins.
whyWrong.B: Both local files are personal: CLAUDE.local.md is meant to be gitignored and .claude/settings.local.json is kept out of git, so neither reaches the other engineers.
whyWrong.D: A project CLAUDE.md is shared, but Claude Code treats it as context, not enforced configuration. Blocking an edit regardless of what the model decides needs a hook, and a repeatable multi-step workflow is better carried as a skill.

questions.mindset: Hand off team knowledge in versioned, project-scoped files: project skills and committed project settings, not anyone's personal config.

questions.stem: An agent that drafts settlement letters for insurance adjusters has been live for a month. The operations dashboard tracks uptime, HTTP error rate and p95 latency, and all three are green. The sponsor wants to catch any drop in letter quality early, before it shows up as complaints. Which TWO additional monitoring signals are MOST effective? Choose TWO.

options.text: Average letter length in characters, tracked daily and reported to the sponsor as the main indicator of letter quality.
How often adjusters heavily edit or discard the drafts they receive, trended over time and broken down by claim type.
Total API requests per hour, with an alert whenever volume drops below the normal range for that day of the week.
A confidence score from 1 to 10 that the drafting model assigns to itself at the end of each letter it writes.
Regular grading of a random sample of production letters against the same rubric, using the same graders as the offline eval suite.

questions.explanation: System metrics (uptime, errors, latency) can stay green while quality slips. Two signals track quality directly: **how often users override or discard outputs**, a leading sign of drift that segments well, and **production sampling graded the same way as the offline suite**, so live numbers can be compared with test numbers.

whyWrong.A: Length can change for harmless reasons and stay stable while content gets worse, so it is at best a weak proxy and a poor main quality indicator.
whyWrong.C: Request volume is a usage and availability signal. It says nothing about whether the letters are correct.
whyWrong.D: A model grading its own confidence is poorly calibrated and is no substitute for independent grading.

questions.mindset: Monitor quality directly: user override rates plus production samples graded like your evals.

questions.stem: A high-volume claims-summarisation service keeps a long, unchanging policy section at the start of its system prompt and uses prompt caching. In the last iteration a developer added the current date and the adjuster's name to the top of the system prompt so summaries could be personalised. The eval suite still passes, and the error-rate and latency dashboards are flat, but the finance partner reports that monthly API spend has more than doubled while request volume is unchanged. What should the team do FIRST to diagnose and prevent this class of regression?

options.text: Move the summaries to a smaller, cheaper model, since the eval suite shows the quality target has enough headroom to absorb a small drop in accuracy on this task.
Add an instruction to the system prompt asking Claude to write shorter summaries, since output tokens cost more per token than input and are the easiest cost to cut.
Compare cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens across the release, move the date and name below the static prefix, and alert on cache hit rate.
Raise the cache lifetime from the default 5 minutes to 1 hour so each cached prefix is reused by many more requests before it expires and has to be written again.

questions.explanation: The cache prefix is built in order (tools, then system, then messages) and a change at any point **invalidates everything from that point on**. Putting the date and adjuster name at the top of the system prompt makes the prefix differ for every adjuster and every day, so the long policy text can no longer be shared across requests: most calls now write it to cache instead of reading it. The usage fields show this directly: cache_read_input_tokens collapses and cache_creation_input_tokens rises. The fix is to keep static content first and variable content after it, then monitor cache hit rate per release so a quality-neutral prompt edit cannot silently break the budget again.

whyWrong.A: The extra cost comes from a lost cache, not from the model tier. Changing models to pay for a bug adds quality risk and is a much larger change than restoring the prefix order.
whyWrong.B: Output length did not change in this release. The spend increase is on input tokens that stopped being served from cache, so shorter summaries would barely move the bill.
whyWrong.D: A longer lifetime only helps when the identical prefix comes back. With the adjuster name and date ahead of the policy text, the policy can't be shared across adjusters or days whatever the TTL, and 1-hour cache writes cost 2x the base input price versus 1.25x for 5-minute writes.

questions.mindset: Monitor cost drivers such as cache hit rate per release: a prompt edit that leaves quality unchanged can still break the budget.

questions.stem: A support assistant has run for four months. Production sampling has flagged 140 failed responses this month, and the team has capacity for one focused improvement this sprint. A senior executive has forwarded two recent failures he found embarrassing. How should the team choose what to work on in this iteration?

options.text: Fix the two cases the executive forwarded first, since visible complaints from leadership carry the most business risk.
Rewrite the system prompt from scratch to address all flagged failures at once, then spot-check a handful of cases before release.
Upgrade the service to a more capable model, since a stronger model is likely to fix many failure categories in a single release.
Cluster the failures by root cause, rank clusters by frequency and business impact, fix the top one, and add its cases to the eval suite.

questions.explanation: Iteration works best as **error analysis**: group failures by root cause, size the groups, fix the most valuable one, and add those cases to the suite so the fix is measured and protected from regressions. The executive's cases go into the analysis too, sized by the same rules.

whyWrong.A: Two loud cases may be rare. Fixing them first can leave the biggest source of failures untouched.
whyWrong.B: Rewriting everything at once makes it impossible to tell which change helped or hurt, and a spot-check won't catch regressions.
whyWrong.C: A model change is a big, costly release on its own. Without knowing the root causes, there's no evidence it fixes them.

questions.mindset: Iterate from error analysis: cluster, size, fix the biggest group, and lock it in with eval cases.

questions.stem: A revised system prompt for a production claims-intake agent has passed the full eval suite and beats the current version. The team wants to release it with the LOWEST risk to live users. Which TWO practices should they follow? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep the prompt under version control with the code and configuration, so the previous version can be restored quickly if needed.
Edit the prompt directly in the live configuration console, so users get the improvement without waiting for a deployment cycle.
Skip any further production comparison, because a passing result on the full eval suite already proves the change is safe to ship.
Send a slice of live traffic to the new prompt first and compare its monitoring signals with the current version before cutover.
Bundle the pending model upgrade into the same release, so stakeholders have only a single change to review and absorb.

questions.explanation: Treat a prompt change like any software release. **Version it** so rollback is quick and the change is traceable. **Roll it out gradually**, comparing live signals (quality samples, override rates, stop reasons, cost) against the current version, because evals can't cover every real input.

whyWrong.B: Untracked live edits remove the review, the audit trail and easy rollback.
whyWrong.C: Evals cover a finite set of cases. Production traffic can still show behavior the suite never saw.
whyWrong.E: Changing the prompt and the model at once makes it impossible to tell which one caused a regression.

questions.mindset: Prompt changes are releases: version them, roll them out gradually, and change one thing at a time.

questions.stem: A team plans to have an LLM grader score a weekly sample of production answers against a rubric, and to report the result to the sponsor as the system's quality KPI. Before the team relies on this number, which step is MOST important?

options.text: Use the same model and system prompt that produced the answers, so the grader shares exactly the same context as the original call.
Compare the grader's scores with expert labels on a sample, refine the rubric until they agree well enough, and recheck regularly.
Raise the sample from 2% to 20% of weekly traffic, so random noise in individual grades averages out over a much larger number.
Have the grader return just a single overall score with no rubric, so grading stays fast and the KPI is easy to explain.

questions.explanation: An LLM grader is only useful if it **agrees with expert judgment**. Calibrate it against human labels, write a clear rubric, check that it gives consistent results, and recheck over time. Then the KPI means what the sponsor thinks it means.

whyWrong.A: Anthropic's guidance suggests a grader separate from the model being evaluated. Reusing the same setup risks sharing its blind spots.
whyWrong.C: A bigger sample cuts random noise but not systematic bias. A badly calibrated grader just gives a more precise wrong number.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the rubric makes grades less consistent and harder to trust, which is the opposite of what a KPI needs.

questions.mindset: Calibrate automated graders against human judgment before turning their scores into a KPI.

questions.stem: Six months after launch, the HR director wants the benefits Q&A assistant to "also submit leave requests on employees' behalf". Engineering offers to add a submission tool next sprint. What is the BEST lifecycle response?

options.text: Treat it as a new capability: run discovery and design on approvals and permissions, add action cases to evals, and pilot it.
Add the submission tool next sprint exactly as proposed, then watch the support channel for complaints once the feature is live.
Decline the request, because the original discovery scoped the assistant to answering questions only, and widening scope adds risk.
Design a separate autonomous multi-agent system for HR transactions with its own planner, so the Q&A assistant stays untouched.

questions.explanation: Moving from **answering** to **acting** changes the risk. The lifecycle starts again on a small scale: discovery (what success means, who approves, what happens on errors), design (permissions and safeguards), new eval cases for actions, and a pilot before broad release.

whyWrong.B: Shipping an action-taking tool with no criteria or evals and waiting for complaints is the riskiest path for actions that affect employees.
whyWrong.C: Scope can grow. The right response is to run the change through the lifecycle, not to refuse it.
whyWrong.D: A separate multi-agent system is over-engineered before discovery has even shown what the feature needs.

questions.mindset: A new capability, especially one that takes actions, restarts the lifecycle loop on a small scale.
